title: Re-evaluation of xanthan gum (E 415) as a food additive
authors: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS), Mortensen A, Aguilar F, Crebelli R, Di Domenico A, Frutos MJ, et al.
funder: European Food Safety Authority; requestor: European Commission; question number EFSA-Q-2011-00514.
result: Xanthan gum is a high molecular weight polysaccharide produced by pure-culture fermentation of a carbohydrate with strains of Xanthomonas campestris and recovered with ethanol or propan-2-ol; a backbone of beta-(1->4) linked D-glucose carries on every second glucose a C3 trisaccharide side chain of beta-D-mannose-(1->4)-beta-D-glucuronic acid-(1->2)-alpha-D-mannose, with pyruvate on 30 to 50% of the terminal mannose residues as a 4,6-acetal and acetyl on 60 to 70% of the internal mannose residues; reported molecular weight about 1,000,000 to 2,000,000 g/mol; CAS 11138-66-2. Authorised in 79 EU food categories, mostly at quantum satis as a Group I additive, with 10,000 mg/kg in jams, jellies and marmalades individually or combined with other listed gums, 1,200 mg/L in dietary foods for infants and young children for special medical purposes (categories 13.1.5.1 and 13.1.5.2) and no use in jelly mini-cups. Xanthan gum is unlikely to be absorbed intact and is not metabolised by gastrointestinal enzymes, but is partially fermented by intestinal microbiota to short-chain fatty acids; in rats given 14C-labelled xanthan gum, unchanged or only slightly modified polysaccharide accounted for about 98% of faecal radioactivity and a maximum of 15% of the label was metabolised to carbon dioxide within 100 hours. Refined non-brand-loyal exposure reached 64 mg/kg body weight per day in children aged 3 to 9 years, 38 mg/kg bw per day for child consumers of food supplements and, for brand-loyal consumers of foods for special medical purposes, 115 mg/kg bw per day in infants aged 12 weeks to 11 months. Repeated intake by adults of up to 15,000 mg per person per day (214 mg/kg bw per day) for at least ten days was well tolerated, with abdominal discomfort in some individuals, judged undesirable but not adverse. The Panel concluded that there is no need for a numerical ADI and no safety concern at the refined exposure; the re-evaluation does not apply to infants under 12 weeks of age. Human studies cited: five men took 10.4 to 12.9 g per day (149 to 184 mg/kg bw per day) for 23 consecutive days, with raised faecal wet and dry weight, shorter transit time, serum cholesterol 10% lower (p < 0.05) and higher faecal bile acid concentrations (p < 0.05) (Eastwood et al., 1987); 18 healthy men took 15 g per day for 10 days, with increases in stool output (p < 0.01), frequency of defaecation (p < 0.05) and flatulence (p < 0.01) and variable effects on transit time (Daly et al., 1993). Studies submitted by Abbott Nutrition in neonatal piglets dosed 0, 375, 750 or 3,750 mg/kg bw per day for 20 days from postnatal day 2 gave a NOEL of 375 mg/kg bw per day from faecal changes and a NOAEL of 750 mg/kg bw per day from minimal to moderate intestinal histopathology at the high dose; post-marketing surveillance by Abbott Nutrition of hydrolysate formulae containing about 750 mg/L over an estimated 131 million patient treatment days reported fewer than one adverse event report per 10,000 patient treatment days. JECFA (1986) and the SCF (1990) allocated an ADI 'not specified'. Use as an ingredient of food for patients with dysphagia is noted. Reports of 22 infants who developed late-onset necrotising enterocolitis after a xanthan gum-containing thickener (Beal et al., 2012; Woods et al., 2012) were judged not related to the food additive use of xanthan gum in the manufacture of infant formula, the ingested doses being unknown but expected in gram amounts. Recommendations: revise the lead limit and add limits for mercury, cadmium and arsenic in the EU specifications, and collect usage data, since Mintel lists xanthan gum in more products than industry reported.
